item.title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: classical coefficients across ionization and magnetization
item.description: arXiv:2610.30303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical transport of magnetic field and electron energy in a plasma requires the use of coefficients that depend on plasma ionization $Z$ and magnetization $\chi$. This paper explains these scalings through studying the electron velocities responsible for each transport process. Both electron-electron collisions and magnetization affect higher velocity electron populations preferentially, lowering the carrier velocities; transport carried by a high energy electron population is therefore more suppressed by both electron-electron collisions and magnetization than transport carried by lower velocities. Carrier Hall parameters $\psi=\chi f(Z)$ are defined for each coefficient such that magnetization can be described independent of ionization. An analytic idealized coefficient with a single rigid carrier velocity reproduces many of the characteristics of the coefficients, in particular thermal conductivity, but overestimates plasma magnetization due to magnetization itself lowering the carrier velocity. A single moving carrier model improves agreement, but cannot describe the smoothness of the Righi-Leduc coefficient, which originates from being an average over a range of carrier velocities. This is the first paper in a 3-part series; the subsequent papers will extend the carrier picture to non-local heat-flux (paper 2) and non-local magnetic field evolution (paper 3).
item.dc:creator: C. A. Walsh

item.title: Evolution of Jeans instability in nonthermal magnetized complex plasmas
item.description: arXiv:2610.30332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical Jeans instability framework provides a conceptual foundation for understanding self-gravitational collapse and subsequent star formation in interstellar environments. However, cosmic plasmas are inherently magnetized and frequently collisionless, exhibiting significant departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium. While linear theories predict initial instability thresholds, they fail to track the long-term nonlinear runaway dynamics. We present a fluid simulation investigating the nonlinear evolution of the Jeans instability in a magnetized tricomponent complex (dusty) plasma. The constituent nonthermal electrons and ions are governed by the $\kappa$-distribution law, while the heavier dust grains are treated in a fluid framework, coupled with a uniform ambient magnetic field. The numerical architecture utilizes a fourth-order finite difference method (FDM) for spatial gradients and a second-order leap-frog time-integration scheme. We systematically investigate the complex interplay among the self-gravitational attraction, nonthermal electrostatic screening, and magnetic pressure across a wide range of magnetic field strengths and degrees of nonthermality. It is found that enhanced nonthermality accelerates structural localization, while the magnetic field introduces a critical pressure barrier that suppresses the instability. In highly magnetized environments, thermal and nonthermal systems exhibit identical growth rate characteristics, indicating that magnetic pressure dominates the nonthermal thermostatistics in the strong magnetic regime. This study develops a comprehensive and numerically robust framework to understand early-stage star formation and evolution processes in nonthermal astrophysical media.
item.dc:creator: Dipankar Ray, Pralay Kumar Karmakar, Bharati Kakad, Amar Kakad

item.title: A novel mechanism for spontaneous ExB shear layer formation in scrape-off-layer plasmas
item.description: arXiv:2610.30343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a novel mechanism for spontaneous shear-flow generation in the scrape-off layer (SOL) of magnetically confined plasmas, arising at abrupt changes in the sheath connection length $L_\parallel$. Such transitions occur naturally in the Wendelstein 7-X stellarator. Applying a critical balance treatment for interchange turbulence, we find that $L_\parallel$ sets the equilibrium pressure gradient and hence the radial electric field away from the transition, producing an $E\times B$ shear around the transition comparable to the turbulence growth rate. High-fidelity simulations are shown to be consistent with the theoretical prediction.
item.dc:creator: Brendan Shanahan, Eduardo Rodriguez

item.title: Robust PCA Study of TEM Images of Gold Nanospheres: Stable and Dynamic Closed Knot-Like Phase-Space Loops
item.description: arXiv:2610.30367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, we apply Robust PCA to transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of gold nanoparticles (GNPs) to decompose their geometrical, topological, and dynamical organization into static and dynamic knot-like phase-space loops. Dynamic loops show higher crossing numbers and longer rope lengths, while static loops show higher mean curvature. Although most Alexander determinants were D(t)=1 with isolated values of D(t)=3 at smaller nanoparticle diameters, implying that geometrical complexity does not require topological complexity. The different writhe signs indicate opposite handedness and distinct phase-space geometries in static and dynamic cases. For both static and dynamic knot-like loops, the graphs show an inverse relationship between mean curvature and mean torsion. Flatter trajectories occur at high curvature, and more torsional twisting occurs at low curvature. The small changes in Moffatt-Ricca helicities (~10^-14<<0) are due to circulation-dependent scaling, yet Moffatt-Ricca helicities still follow the same self-linking trend in both static and dynamic configurations. As nanoparticle diameter increases, the dynamic knot-like loops show stronger Kelvin-like spectral localization and smaller minimum self-approach distances, indicating more concentrated spatial modes and tighter geometric folding. At the same time, the decreasing CTEI suggests reduced global phase-space organization. These contrasting trends indicate that the geometrical organization tends to be less global and coherent, and more localized and mode-specific. These results show that the PCA-reconstructed phase space could serve as a mathematical analog to Kelvin's aether, because all disturbances exhibit similar topological configurations with varying degrees of geometric difference.
item.dc:creator: Mehmet F. Yilmaz, Bekir Karlik

item.title: Experimental evidence of forward energy transfer induced by core-edge coupling in multiscale tokamak turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.30638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turbulence in magnetically confined plasmas is inherently quasi-two-dimensional and can exhibit both inverse and forward energy transfer across scales. Experimental evidence for cross-scale energy transfer in the hot plasma core has, however, remained scarce. Understanding such energy transfer is crucial because it governs turbulent transport, which directly impacts confinement quality of fusion plasmas. Here we report experimental evidence consistent with forward energy transfer associated with core-edge coupling in tokamak turbulence. We combined multichannel collective Thomson scattering (CTS) and radially localized Doppler backscattering (DBS) to resolve cross-scale fluctuation dynamics. The results reveal that a quasi-coherent mode (QCM) originating from the edge is also present in the core and resonantly couples with broadband turbulence, producing significant forward energy transfer and characteristic secondary instabilities. These combined measurements indicate that quasi-two-dimensional tokamak turbulence can support a net energy transfer from ion to electron scales through cross-scale wave-wave interactions, contrary to the inverse cascade paradigm of idealized two-dimensional turbulence. Such a plasma regime is attractive for fusion reactors, as it avoids large edge-localized modes (ELMs) that damage first-wall components and maintains high confinement quality even in the presence of high-Z impurities.

item.title: Self-gravitating isothermal equilibria in Eddington-inspired Born--Infeld gravity: exact planar sheets and the Bonnor--Ebert critical mass
item.description: arXiv:2610.30716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study self-gravitating fluid equilibria in the Newtonian limit of Eddington-inspired Born--Infeld (EiBI) gravity, in which the Poisson equation acquires a term proportional to the Laplacian of the density. We show that this term is equivalent, for arbitrary flows, to an effective pressure $p+\chi\rho^2/8$, so that equilibrium and radial stability reduce exactly to Newtonian problems with a modified equation of state. For pressure-bounded isothermal spheres we compute the EiBI generalization of the Bonnor--Ebert critical mass as a function of the single parameter $\varepsilon=\chi P_{\rm ext}/4c_s^4$, and confirm each change of stability with a radial-pulsation analysis. Near $\varepsilon=0$ the critical mass grows as $M_{\rm BE}(1+5.74\,\varepsilon)$. For $\varepsilon>0.0302$ no isothermal sphere is radially unstable, so a positive EiBI parameter removes the Bonnor--Ebert instability; for smaller positive $\varepsilon$ a stable high-density branch supported by the EiBI pressure follows the unstable one. For $\varepsilon<-0.154$ the mass limit is set instead by the vanishing of the central effective sound speed, and is a loss of equilibrium rather than an instability. In planar geometry the same reduction yields an exact first integral, closed-form isothermal sheets with a maximum column density $2c_s^2/\sqrt{\pi G|\chi|}$ for $\chi<0$, and a complete classification of adiabatic $\gamma=3$ sheets.
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Chakrabarti

item.title: Nonlinear Drift Waves and Electrostatic Density Cavities in Upper Ionosphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.30826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear drift waves are investigated to explain the mechanism for the creation of one dimensional (1D) and two dimensional (2D) electrostatic density cavities in the presence of density gradient in direction perpendicular to the geomagnetic field. Ion motion along field lines has to be neglected for the formation of density depletion because nonlinear contribution of their parallel motion overcomes the effect of drift waves which create negative nonlinear potential. It is pointed out that a straightforward but appropriate model for drift waves can explain the generation of density cavities having widths in xy-plane if the external magnetic field is assumed to be along z-axis i.e. ${\bf B}_0 = B_0 \hat{z}$. The general nonlinear equation for drift waves takes the form of Zakharov-Kuznetson (ZK) equation when ion nonlinear vorticity term is ignored and it admits the solution in the form of 2D solitary wave. In 1D case, the ZK equation reduces to Korteweg de Vries (KdV) equation which admits solution in the form of 1D soliton. In both cases, the nonlinear potential becomes negative. The order of magnitude of the amplitude and width of density cavities is found to be in agreement with the satellite observations in upper ionosphere.
item.dc:creator: Hamid Saleem, Usman Saeed

item.title: On Spurious Mesh-Scale Oscillations Associated with Resonance-Cone Regimes in Wave-Plasma Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.31021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spurious mesh-scale oscillations can compromise frequency-domain finite-element simulations of electromagnetic wave propagation in magnetized cold plasmas. We investigate their origin and mitigation through a verification framework combining a mixed N\'ed\'elec-Lagrange solver, a waveport accommodating non-orthogonal modes in anisotropic media, and an analytical generalized Fresnel benchmark at a vacuum-plasma interface. Comparisons with this benchmark show that the observed oscillations occur in resonance-cone regimes and are absent from the analytical fields, confirming their numerical origin. Systematic tests assess the effects of approximation order, variational formulation, mesh geometry, and numerical collisionality. Plane-wave residual and Fourier spectral analyses suggest that local mesh variations induce spectral coupling to additional wavevector components, predominantly populating the dispersion branches in collisionless resonance-cone regimes where the reduced scalar equation loses ellipticity. Uniform rectangular grids recover the analytical wave structure, further supporting the role of mesh geometry and symmetry. However, strict symmetry requirements limit the applicability of this approach, motivating numerical regularization. In resonance-cone regimes, introducing sufficient numerical collisionality suppresses the mesh-scale oscillations, yielding smooth electric-field solutions and reducing the error relative to the analytical benchmark. For one resonance-cone benchmark configuration, the error-minimizing damping decreases with mesh refinement according to an empirical $Z_{\mathrm n}\propto h^{1.48}$ scaling, sustaining error reduction consistent with second-order convergence and avoiding the accuracy limit imposed by fixed collisionality. ...
item.dc:creator: Hugo Bergerioux, Mario Merino

item.title: Synthetic 2D magnetic turbulence with controlled island structuring
item.description: arXiv:2610.31367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic turbulence remains up to this day not fully understood, despite its important role in the behavior of plasmas. A recurring ingredient in plasma turbulence is the spontaneous formation and evolution of plasmoids. These represent magnetic islands on current sheets in two-dimensional turbulent magnetic fields that are consistently found in high-resolution direct numerical simulations (DNSs) using a magnetohydrodynamic description. However, such simulations require considerable amounts of computational power. Synthetic turbulence models provide an alternative, cheap approach to the generation of fully-developed turbulent fields. In this work, we first present an extension of our open-source, general synthetic turbulence BxC toolkit that is specifically tailored to generate 2D turbulent magnetic fields. We then use a novel physically motivated, but purely geometric construction that generates current sheet island chains, which results in fields that visually match the ones obtained through DNSs. We show how this construction affects the magnetic field lines and find a correlation with the formation of magnetic O-points and X-points. The magnetic flux and size of the islands in the field are found to match well with theoretical scaling laws. Lastly, we show BxC's capabilities by generating a 2D $N\times N$ turbulent magnetic field of resolution $N = 100000$, going beyond the state-of-the-art reached by simulations, on a single CPU with modest computational resources. Our construction maintains direct control over the inertial range, and allows to make morphological changes to the plasmoids and fields, demonstrating plasmoid appearance, disappearance and merging.
item.dc:creator: Yari De Paep, Daniela Maci, Rony Keppens

item.title: GEM-PIC-RZ: a Galilean electromagnetic particle-in-cell code in quasi-cylindrical geometry with nonuniform grids
item.description: arXiv:2610.31622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators span scales from the micrometre wavelength of the driving laser to acceleration lengths of millimetres or metres. Full particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations resolve the laser carrier but are constrained by the Courant condition, whereas quasi-static models are computationally efficient but do not resolve it. We present GEM-PIC-RZ, a quasi-cylindrical implementation of the Galilean electromagnetic PIC scheme. The method retains the slow evolution of the forward field and therefore resolves the laser carrier while allowing a propagation step governed by the evolution of the laser and plasma rather than by the cell size. User-defined nonuniform grids and a charge-conserving regularization of the bubble closure support efficient simulations across these scales. Comparisons with the full PIC code FBPIC show agreement for the laser wake, the depletion and redshift of a few-cycle pulse, and ionization injection; the measured CPU time is about 2\,\% of that for FBPIC in the reported runs; the injected charge carries a model uncertainty of about 15\,\% from the regularization. An envelope model, in contrast, underestimates the depletion of the few-cycle pulse fivefold. Self-injection in a sharp density down-ramp is not yet reproduced and remains an open problem.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Pukhov

item.title: First Results of Calculation of the Dayside Magnetopause Reconnection Rate with TRACERS
item.description: arXiv:2610.30517v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantifying the rate of reconnection remains a key challenge in the study of geomagnetic storms. In this study, we present the first results from the new Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites (TRACERS) mission to calculate the reconnection rate from dispersed ion populations measured in the cusp, using previously developed methodology. We study ion dispersion events in two storms. During the first storm, which occurred on September 30, 2025, 21 dispersion events were identified in TRACERS 2 ion data as a combined result of geospace dynamics and the spacecraft cusp encounters. Throughout this time when ion dispersion was detected by TRACERS , the reconnection rate is calculated and is shown to track reasonably well with another measure of geomagnetic activity, the Cross Polar Cap Potential (CPCP) as obtained by the Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN). The dispersions are correlated with the smoothed CPCP, and a correlation of $r^2=0.62$ was found using the dispersions from the onset and main phase of the storm. The correlation disappears when including dispersions from the recovery period. The distribution of reconnection rates throughout this storm lies generally between 0.1 - 1.5 mV/m, slightly lower than previous reconnection rates calculated with DMSP, but consistent with in-situ observations made with Polar. In this work, we also apply a previously developed automatic identification algorithm for ion-energy cusp dispersion to TRACERS, with the intent that it may serve as a tool for future statistical analysis as the data volume becomes too large to manually review.

item.title: Geodesic torsion of the magnetic field line and other predictors of coil non-planarity in QI stellarators
item.description: arXiv:2604.26763v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stellarator magnetic fields are often realized with non-planar modular coils with their out-of-plane bending being one of the main engineering challenges. We ask whether the non planarity of the fialment can be predicted from the equilibrium alone. We look at a dataset of coils for stellarator equilibira and find that the geodesic torsion of the magnetic field line is a strong and robust predictor in a wide range of coil feasibility requirements. We compare the performance of the geodesic torsion against other equilibrium and surface geometry properties and find it to be a superior predictorv hardly replaceable by other quantities we considered in this dataset. The ranking it induces also reproduces the ordering of four published configurations --- precise QA, precise QI at nfp 2 and 3, and W7-X. Our conclusions suggest that geodesic torsion of the magnetic field line may be considered as a cheap and robust candidate for a stage-one non-planarity proxy.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Pavone, Sehyun Kwak, Felix Warmer

item.title: Filament Formation via Collision-induced Magnetic Reconnection -- Kinematic Features
item.description: arXiv:2609.16205v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Collision-induced Magnetic Reconnection (CMR) mechanism has recently been proposed as a filament formation model that emphasizes the active role of magnetic fields. To enable better observational tests with data from modern telescopes, we provide more specific observable predictions for filaments formed via CMR. Two types of CMR kinematics are revealed in position-velocity (PV) diagrams. First, due to the nature of CMR, the midplane contains a {\it converging motion} close to the filament and two {\it diverging motions} farther from the filament. They exhibit a blueshift, redshift, blueshift, redshift (BRBR) velocity pattern along the line-of-sight when the collision midplane is inclined, giving rise to a special pattern in the PV-diagram. Second, the longitudinal PV-diagram along the filament spine exhibits a velocity oscillating pattern, which is currently attributed to the magnetic transport of gas clumps in the {\it converging motion}. The first type of pattern involves emission primarily outside the filament, which can be confused with the environment. The second type, however, mainly emerges from gas inside the filament, thus more robust for observational tests. Both the integral-shaped filament and the Stick filament in the Orion A cloud show the velocity oscillation in PV-diagrams, although the spatial oscillation frequency and their velocity spread differ.
item.dc:creator: Shuo Kong, Griselda Arroyo-Ch\'avez, Volker Ossenkopf-Okada, H\'ector G. Arce, Ralf S. Klessen, Duo Xu, Szu-Ting Chen

item.title: Energy-dependent trapping of backscattered helium during magnetron sputtering growth: A molecular dynamics study
item.description: arXiv:2610.13509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Helium incorporation during magnetron sputtering can strongly affect thin film growth and lead to the formation of gas/solid nanocomposites and nanoporous structures. Here, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are used to investigate the trapping mechanism of helium atoms (He) and the subsequent formation of He bubbles during the sputter deposition of aluminum (Al) and titanium (Ti) thin films. The simulations account for the kinetic energy distributions of sputtered metal atoms and backscattered gas species. Results indicate that He is efficiently incorporated into the growing films, leading to the formation of high-pressure, dense He bubbles, with a much higher He-to-metal atomic ratio in Ti ($\sim$ 60%) than in Al ($\sim$ 12%). More importantly, the simulations reveal a clear energy dependence of He trapping in Ti: background He atoms at thermal energies are essentially not incorporated, whereas efficient trapping starts at an incident energy of approximately 20 eV and increases up to a saturation regime near 100 eV. Simulated thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) further reveals distinct release mechanisms in the two investigated metals: He desorption from Al occurs at higher temperatures and is preceded by the removal of surface Al atoms, whereas He and Ti atom desorption starts continuously around 950 K, leading to a porous structure. Comparative simulations with argon (Ar) demonstrate negligible trapping even at comparable kinetic energy or momentum, showing that neither parameter alone accounts for the strong He incorporation observed in Ti. The above results are in very good agreement with what is reported in literature for low-kinetic energy He ion implantation in metal surfaces, suggesting similar insertion mechanisms. They clarify the atomistic conditions governing noble gas trapping during film growth and provide a basis for controlling He incorporation and porosity in films synthesized by magnetron sputtering.
item.dc:creator: Pascal Brault (GREMI, MS4ALL), Anne-Lise Thomann (GREMI), Alejandro Borroto (GREMI)
